summary: For ages 8-9, build fluency in moving BETWEEN representations of multiplication, fractions, and decimals: a sharing story, a fraction diagram, a number line, an area/bar model, and a written equation are different views of ONE structure, not separate procedures. Two anchoring ideas: a decimal and its fraction (0.3 and 3/10) name the SAME number — one point/magnitude on a line, not two kinds of thing — and an area or strip model must be read as quantities (each part has a value relative to the whole, and the parts' values combine into the total), not as a bare count of pieces. The recurring failure is treating each representation as its own routine (the area model 'for pictures', the written method 'for answers'); good teaching keeps asking 'what's the same across these, and where does each number live in the other?'
misconceptions: Treats a decimal and its fraction as different kinds of number that can't share a point (0.3 ≠ 3/10 'because one's a decimal')
Applies whole-number thinking to decimals (0.35 > 0.5 'because 35 > 5'; reads 0.3 as 'three')
Reads the area/bar model as a separate procedure from the written method, unable to say how they show the same calculation
Counts parts of a diagram without seeing that numerator and denominator name a single quantity

activities.title: Same point on the line: 0.3 and 3/10
steps: Mark where 0.3 goes on a number line from 0 to 1, then mark where 3/10 goes, and say whether they land on the same point.
Explain in your own words why both are 'three tenths of the way from 0 to 1' — the same magnitude shown two ways.
Place 0.35 and 0.5 on the line and explain which is bigger and why (0.35 is less than 0.5), checking against a tenths/hundredths grid.
Apply the same reasoning to a fresh pair, e.g. 0.27 and 27/100: place both on the line and explain the equivalence.
activities.insight: A decimal and its equivalent fraction are the same number — the same position/magnitude on the line — so notation (decimal vs fraction) is not identity; magnitude is.

activities.title: Where do 80 and 12 live? Linking the area model and the written method for 4×23
steps: Split 23 into 20 and 3 and draw an area model (rectangle) for 4×23, showing the two regions.
Point to the region that is 4×20 and the region that is 4×3, and state their values (80 and 12).
Write out the written method for 4×23 beside the rectangle and match each partial product to its region; check the two regions sum to 92.
Say out loud what is the same and what is different between the picture and the algorithm.
activities.insight: The area model and the written method are one structure viewed two ways: each partial product (4×20=80 and 4×3=12) is a region of the rectangle, and 80+12=92 is the total.

activities.title: One sharing story, three ways
steps: Tell a sharing story that 6÷4 (or another division) could represent.
Draw a fraction diagram for it and write the matching division equation.
Say what each number in the equation represents in both the story and the diagram.
Translate the other way too: given a diagram, write the equation; given an equation, draw the diagram.
activities.insight: A real-world situation, its diagram, and its symbolic equation are different views of the same quantity; fluency means moving in BOTH directions and naming what each number refers to.

activities.title: Convince a doubter: dialogue and discussion
steps: Respond to a partner (classmate, adult, or in-role character) who insists '0.3 and 3/10 must be different — one's a decimal!' and argue, with the number line and a tenths grid, that they share one point.
Have the partner point at an area model for 4×23 and ask 'which bit is the 80, which is the 12?' — answer by tracing each to its region and to the written method.
Explain your reasoning aloud rather than just stating an answer.
activities.insight: Being asked to defend equivalence and shared structure can push the child to articulate WHY representations coincide, not just that they do.

checkQuestion: A classmate says: '0.3 and 3/10 are different numbers — 0.3 is a decimal and 3/10 is a fraction, so they'd go in different places on a number line.' Do you agree? Show me where each one goes on a line from 0 to 1, and explain what you find. Then tell me how you'd convince the classmate.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child placing 0.3 and 3/10 at the SAME point and explaining they are the same number/magnitude shown two ways (three tenths of the way from 0 to 1), rather than treating decimal and fraction as different kinds of thing living in different places.
